why:
A semiconductor carries current by TWO kinds of charge carrier, not one. Section 14.4 states that there are two different types of charge carriers in a semiconductor, one the electron and the other the hole, and that the current through a semiconductor is carried by two types of charge carriers which move in opposite directions; Fig. 14.8 accordingly labels both an electron current and a hole current in the same crystal. Electrons, being negatively charged, drift towards the positive terminal, while holes carry an effective positive charge and drift towards the negative terminal, so the two contributions add. Hence conduction is due to both electrons and holes.

Why the others fail: "electrons" alone and "holes" alone are each only half the mechanism — in a pure crystal the two carrier densities are in fact equal, \(n_{h} = n_{e}\), so neither can be dismissed, and even in a doped crystal the minority carrier still conducts. "None of these" is contradicted by the whole chapter, which exists to explain how a semiconductor conducts.

The phrase "energy levels of holes" is the chapter's own name for the extra levels that a trivalent (acceptor) dopant introduces. Section 14.5 says of a p-type crystal that the impurity levels are created just above the valence band in the band gap, and that electrons from the valence band can easily occupy these levels and conduct electricity. Fig. 14.14, the schematic band structure of a p-type semiconductor, draws exactly one extra line between the two bands, sitting just above the valence band, and labels it "Extra hole energy levels". So these levels lie in the band gap, close to the valence band.

Why the others fail: "in the conduction band" is where a freed electron goes, not a hole. "In the band gap but close to conduction band" is the mirror-image case — Fig. 14.11 gives that position to the "Extra electron energy levels" of an n-type crystal, so it is the answer to the opposite question. "In the valence band" is the one to weigh seriously: the chapter does say that the vacancies are created in the valence band, so that is where a hole itself sits in a pure crystal. But the question asks for the hole ENERGY LEVELS, which is the label the book attaches to the acceptor levels in the gap; if the valence band were meant, the two "band gap" alternatives would be describing nothing in the chapter at all.

[Note: this is the one question in the chapter where the book pulls two ways, and it is worth knowing before you rely on it. The running text defines a hole as the absence of an electron IN THE VALENCE BAND (Sec. 14.4) and repeats in Sec. 14.5 that the holes are created in the valence band, which points to the alternative "in the valence band" — and a second, independent reading of this chapter did settle on that answer for exactly that reason. The answer given here instead follows the book's own naming convention for band diagrams: Sec. 14.5 says the electrons donated by a pentavalent impurity "occupy energy levels which are in the band gap and are close to the conduction band", and Fig. 14.11 labels those "Extra electron energy levels"; Fig. 14.14 labels the mirror-image levels just above the valence band "Extra hole energy levels". So the book names a level after the carrier it supplies, and a question asking for "the energy levels of holes" is asking for that labelled object. Read this as the answer the book intends, not as a settled point of physics.]

Under reverse bias the depletion layer widens and only a leakage current of a few microamperes flows, and Section 14.7 states that this stays practically unchanged as the reverse voltage is increased. It changes only when the reverse bias is raised to a sufficiently large value: the junction then overheats, covalent bonds break, a large number of carriers become available and there is a sudden rise in the current — the avalanche breakdown. Fig. 14.22 marks this point on the reverse axis as the reverse breakdown voltage and Fig. 14.26 marks the region beyond it as the reverse breakdown region. So the abrupt rise happens at the breakdown voltage.

Why the others fail: at 0.0 V the diode is zero biased and Section 14.7 describes a dynamic equilibrium in which the net current across the junction is zero, so nothing rises there. The values 0.3 V and 0.7 V are the two knee voltages quoted in Section 14.7 for germanium and for silicon respectively, and Fig. 14.24 places the knee on the FORWARD bias axis — they belong to the opposite polarity from the one this question asks about.

Section 14.6 says outright that a p-n junction can be used as a one way switch or a gate in an electric circuit: it conducts easily in forward bias and acts as an open switch in reverse bias. Section 14.7 gives the reason — in reverse bias the width of the depletion region increases and the junction behaves like a high resistance, so practically no current flows and only a leakage current of a few microamperes gets through. A switch that is open and passes no useful current is a switch in the off state. Solved Example 14.3 uses the same idealisation, treating the reverse-biased ideal diode as an open path so that its branch drops out of the circuit entirely.

Why the others fail: an on switch is the FORWARD biased case, where the barrier is lowered and a current of a few milliamperes flows. A low resistance is the opposite of what reverse bias produces — the chapter calls the reverse-biased junction a high resistance, and an ideal diode reverse biased has infinite resistance. "None of the above" cannot stand once the open-switch description is available.

Section 14.6 defines the barrier in one sentence: the diffusion of carriers across the junction and the resultant accumulation of positive and negative charges across the junction builds a potential difference across the junction, and this potential difference is called the potential barrier. The Features of the depletion region repeat it — the accumulation of charges on either side of the junction results in forming a potential barrier. The two accumulations are of opposite sign and on opposite sides: electrons crossing to the p-side leave positively charged donor ions behind on the n-side and produce negatively charged acceptor ions on the p-side, which is why Fig. 14.18 shows an electric field pointing across the region. Both signs are needed to set up that field.

Why the others fail: the two "depletion" alternatives name the wrong process. What is depleted near the junction is the FREE carriers — the chapter says the region becomes completely devoid of any charge carriers — and removing free carriers is what exposes the fixed ions rather than what creates the potential difference. "Accumulation of positive charges near the junction" has the right process but only half the picture: a single sign of charge would give no potential difference ACROSS the junction, since the barrier exists precisely because the n-side is left positive with respect to the p-side.
